He spent most of his coaching career at the collegiate level, having served as the head coach of the [[Bowling Green Falcons football|Bowling Green Falcons]] from 2001 to 2002, the [[Utah Utes football|Utah Utes]] from 2003 to 2004, the [[Florida Gators football|Florida Gators]] from 2005 to 2010,{{Cite web |date=December 8, 2010 |title=Meyer stepping down as Florida football coach |url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/news/story?id=5899478 |access-date=July 6, 2025 |website=ESPN.com |language=en |agency=Associated Press}} and the [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State Buckeyes]] from 2012 to 2018.{{cite web |last=Thamel |first=Pete |author-link=Pete Thamel |date=December 4, 2018 |title=Sources: Urban Meyer to step down as Ohio State head coach after Rose Bowl |url=https://sports.yahoo.com/sources-urban-meyer-step-ohio-state-head-coach-123250805.html |access-date=December 4, 2018 |website=Yahoo! Sports}} He retired from coaching in 2019 at the end of the Rose Bowl, and stayed at Ohio State as an assistant athletic director and was also an analyst for [[Fox Sports]], appearing weekly on their ''[[Big Noon Kickoff]]'' pregame show. In 2021, Meyer came out of retirement to take his first [[National Football League]] (NFL) job as head coach of the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]], but was fired 13 games into his first and only season, after going 2–11 and being involved in both on- and off-field controversies. He then went back to Fox Sports to resume his broadcasting career. Meyer was born in [[Toledo, Ohio]]; grew up in [[Ashtabula, Ohio]]; and attended the [[University of Cincinnati]], where he played football as a defensive back. While at the [[University of Florida]], he coached the Gators to two [[BCS National Championship Game]] victories, during the 2006 and 2008 seasons. Meyer's winning percentage through the conclusion of the 2009 season (.842) was the highest among active coaches with a minimum of five full seasons at a [[Football Bowl Subdivision]] (FBS) program."[https://www.si.com/more-sports/2009/12/17/cfb-highlights-lowlights College football: Highlights and lowlights of the decade]," ''Sports Illustrated'' (December 17, 2009). Retrieved December 16, 2021. Following his temporary retirement in 2011, he worked as a college football analyst for the television sports network [[ESPN]] before joining Ohio State to become their head coach. In 2014, he led the Buckeyes to their first [[Big Ten Conference]] title under his tenure as well as the program's eighth [[College football national championships in NCAA Division I FBS|national championship]].{{Cite web |date=January 13, 2015 |title=Ezekiel Elliott's 4 TDs lift Ohio State to inaugural CFP title over Oregon |url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/recap?gameId=400610325 |access-date=July 6, 2025 |website=ESPN.com |language=en |agency=Associated Press}}"[https://www.espn.com/college-football/recap?gameId=400610325]," ' 'ESPN' ' (January 13, 2015). Retrieved December 16, 2021. Meyer is one of four coaches, along with [[Pop Warner]], [[Howard Jones (American football coach)|Howard Jones]], and [[Nick Saban]], to win a major college football national championship at two universities. Florida athletic director Jeremy Foley announced Meyer's resignation on December 8, 2010, but stated that Meyer would remain as the head coach through the Gators' appearance in the [[Outback Bowl]] on January 1, 2011. On November 28, 2011, Meyer accepted the head coach position at Ohio State University. ===Early coaching career=== After playing as a defensive back and placeholder for the University of Cincinnati, Meyer spent one season interning as a defensive back coach at [[St. Xavier High School (Cincinnati)|Saint Xavier High School]] in [[Cincinnati, Ohio]] in 1985, under the mentorship of legendary St. Xavier head coach Steve Rasso, where he met members of the Ohio State coaching staff.Martin, ''Urban's Way'', p. 66. His first collegiate coaching position was a two-year stint as a graduate assistant coaching tight ends at Ohio State under head coach [[Earle Bruce]]. He spent the next thirteen years as an assistant—two at [[Illinois State]], six at [[Colorado State Rams football|Colorado State]], and five at [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football|Notre Dame]]. One of the talents he coached at Colorado State was wide receiver [[Greg Primus]] (3,096 yards and 17 touchdowns in three years). He put up over 1,000 yards receiving from 1990 to 1992 under Meyer's tutelage. At Notre Dame, he coached wide receiver Bobby Brown who would finish his career with 1,521 yards and 12 receiving touchdowns.{{Cite web |title=Bobby Brown College Stats, School, Draft, Gamelog, Splits |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/bobby-brown-2.html |access-date=April 30, 2026 |website=College Football at Sports-Reference.com |language=en}} At Notre Dame in 2000, he coached wide receiver [[David Givens]] who would later be drafted by the [[New England Patriots]].{{cite web |title=2000 Notre Dame Fighting Irish |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/notre-dame/2000.html |access-date=April 30, 2026 |work=College Football at Sports-Reference.com}}{{Cite web |title=David Givens Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/G/GiveDa00.htm |access-date=April 30, 2026 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} In 1990, while still the linebacker coach at Illinois State, he called [[University of Toledo|Toledo]] head coach [[Nick Saban]]'s home and spoke to Saban's wife to inquire if a position was available. Saban, however, never returned the call. Saban later said "I was so kind of caught up and busy with what I was doing, I never really followed up on that. Obviously, that was a huge mistake on my part because the guy's a fantastic coach."{{Cite web |last=Auerbach |first=Nicole |date=December 30, 2014 |title=Nick Saban and Urban Meyer made the best of a 25-year-old oversight |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/ncaaf/2014/12/30/urban-meyer-nick-saban-sugar-bowl-coaches-alabama-ohio-state-college-football-playoff/21061581/ |access-date=July 6, 2025 |website=USA TODAY}} ===Bowling Green=== In 2001, Meyer took his first head coaching job at [[Bowling Green Falcons football|Bowling Green]]. In his first season there, he engineered one of the greatest turnarounds in the [[National Collegiate Athletic Association|NCAA]] football history, going 8–3 and capping off the season with a 56–21 victory over Bowling Green's rival, the University of Toledo Rockets.College Football Data Warehouse, [http://cfbdatawarehouse.com/data/active/b/bowling_green/yearly_results.php?year=2000 Bowling Green Yearly Results: 2000–2004] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304055708/http://cfbdatawarehouse.com/data/active/b/bowling_green/yearly_results.php?year=2000 |date=March 4, 2016 }}. Retrieved September 2, 2009. He also earned Mid-American Conference coach of the year honors.{{Cite web |title=MAC Coach of the Year Winners |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/awards/mac-coy.html |access-date=April 30, 2026 |website=College Football at Sports-Reference.com |language=en}} The next year, Bowling Green finished with a 9–3 record. After a 17–6 overall record, Meyer left for the University of Utah.Liz Abel, "[http://www.unews.utah.edu/p/?r=031706-8 Utah hires Urban Meyer as its new head coach] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060903040204/http://www.unews.utah.edu/p/?r=031706-8 |date=September 3, 2006 }}," press release, University of Utah News Center (December 12, 2002). Retrieved September 1, 2009. He helped turn around a team that had gone 2–9 in 2000 in large part due to quarterback [[Josh Harris (quarterback)|Josh Harris]], a player tailor-made for Meyer's scheme.{{Cite web |last=Alexander |first=Elton |date=November 23, 2011 |title=Urban Meyer pushes his players to new levels, says Josh Harris, former Bowling Green QB |url=https://www.cleveland.com/osu/2011/11/urban_meyer_pushes_his_players.html |access-date=April 30, 2026 |website=The Plain Dealer}} In a part-time play in 2001, Harris passed for 1,022 yards with nine touchdowns and ran for 600 yards and eight touchdowns. The next year, he passed for 2,425 yards with 19 touchdowns and ran for 737 yards with 20 touchdowns. Meyer would later use such quarterbacks as [[Alex Smith]] and [[Tim Tebow]] in a fashion similar to the way Meyer used Harris. ===Utah=== After two seasons at Bowling Green, he took the job at [[Utah Utes football|Utah]] in 2003.Utah Football, [http://utahutes.cstv.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/meyer_urban00.html Player Bio: Urban Meyer] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090101121013/http://utahutes.cstv.com/sports/m-footbl/mtt/meyer_urban00.html |date=January 1, 2009 }}. Urban Meyer is just the guy to take care of this |publisher=Orlando Sentinel |date=September 17, 2010 |access-date=December 16, 2021}} ====2005 season==== {{see also|2005 Florida Gators football team}} In 2005, his first season at Florida, Meyer's [[Florida Gators football|Gators]] team finished the season 9–3 (5–3 in the [[Southeastern Conference]]).{{Cite web |title=2005 Florida Gators Schedule and Results |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/florida/2005-schedule.html |access-date=December 31, 2024 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}} The season included an undefeated record at home and a 31–24 victory against [[2005 Iowa Hawkeyes football team|Iowa]] in the [[2006 Outback Bowl|Outback Bowl]] in [[Tampa, Florida]].{{cite web | title=Football Defeats Iowa In The Outback Bowl, 31-24 | website=Florida Gators Athletics| date=January 2, 2006 | url=https://floridagators.com/news/2006/1/2/9581 | access-date=April 30, 2026}} The Gators would have faced [[2005 LSU Tigers football team|LSU]] in the {{year event|2005|SEC Championship Game}},{{Cite web |date=November 12, 2005 |title=South Carolina derails Gators' SEC East hopes |url=http://www.espn.com/college-football/recap?gameId=253162579 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171027181041/http://www.espn.com/college-football/recap?gameId=253162579 |archive-date=October 27, 2017 |website=ESPN.com|agency=Associated Press}} but they lost to [[2005 South Carolina Gamecocks football team|South Carolina]] and former Florida head coach [[Steve Spurrier]] in the SEC regular-season finale. [[File:Gators at WH 07.jpg|thumb|Meyer at the White House in 2007.]] ====2006 season==== {{see also|2006 Florida Gators football team}} In 2006, Meyer coached the Gators to a 13–1 (8–1 in the SEC) record, with the one loss coming to the [[2006 Auburn Tigers football team|Auburn Tigers]].{{Cite web |title=2006 Florida Gators Schedule and Results |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/florida/2006-schedule.html |access-date=December 31, 2024 |website=[[Sports Reference]] |language=en}} After clinching the SEC East, the Gators won the {{year event|2006|SEC Championship Game}} on December 2 over [[2006 Arkansas Razorbacks football team|Arkansas]] by a score of 38–28. He was released later in the day, and the incident was not announced to the public at the time.{{cite web |last=Low |first=Chris |last2=Schlabach |first2=Mark |author-link2=Mark Schlabach |date=December 6, 2009 |title=Florida: Meyer dehydrated after loss |url=https://www.espn.com/college-football/news/story?id=4719127 |access-date=December 16, 2021 |website=ESPN.com}} On December 26, after discussions with his family, Meyer revealed his medical scare and announced that he would resign as Florida's head coach due to health and family concerns following his team's [[New Year's Day]] Sugar Bowl appearance.
